Osteoarthritis is highly plausible due to common age-related involvement of the first MTP joint (hallux rigidus) and hips/knees, though typically less inflammatory and more insidious. Rheumatoid arthritis fits the symmetrical or migratory polyarticular pattern and can involve the MTP joints early, but isolated left big toe pain is atypical without other small-joint involvement; still plausible given variable presentation. Psoriatic arthritis is considered because of the dactylitis-like or asymmetric oligoarticular pattern—including isolated MTP inflammation—and frequent hip/knee involvement, especially with nail or skin clues not yet elicited. Septic arthritis is lower-confidence but must be ruled out urgently: isolated joint infection rarely presents in multiple joints simultaneously, but hematogenous seeding (e.g., from occult bacteremia) or contiguous spread could involve the big toe and larger joints—though systemic signs (fever, leukocytosis) are absent in this limited history, making it less likely but high-risk if missed."}

CPPD is plausible due to its propensity for chronic, symmetric polyarticular involvement including knees and hips, and occasional MTP involvement; it can mimic OA clinically but often shows chondrocalcinosis on imaging. Erosive OA is supported by the prominent great toe involvement (hallux rigidus) plus axial/hip/knee progression, though typically more hand-dominant. Hemochromatosis-associated arthropathy is less common but fits the chronic, large-joint pattern (especially MCPs, wrists, and second/third MTPs—but first MTP and hips/knees can occur), particularly if there are unreported systemic features (e.g., fatigue, skin bronzing, elevated ferritin); however, lack of corroborating history lowers confidence.
